items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He formed his own group, the Jazz Machine. I was on and off with that group from about ’69 on through the mid ’70s.

ctx.x: He formed his own group, the Jazz Machine. I was on and off with that group from about ’69 on through the mid ’70s. I made several tours, at least two tours of Europe and two tours of the Far East with Jones, or maybe I’m confusing with the Thad Jones – Mel Lewis Orchestra. I made at least one tour of Japan with Elvin, one tour of South America, and one tour of Europe. That’s a playing experience that any saxophonist would treasure, would feel that something was missed if they didn’t play with Elvin at least one…

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: If I didn’t get enough playing in, improvising with the Basie band, I sure made up for it with Elvin.

ctx.x: Oh yeah we had some times. If I didn’t get enough playing in, improvising with the Basie band, I sure made up for it with Elvin.
I guess so, yeah. You had the liberty to play as long as you wanted.

items.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: For one thing it was Thad, and Hank, and Frank West and Frank Foster.

ctx.x: Mhmm. That’s the cover. And do you recall any highlights, any of the session?

Well, quite a few. For one thing it was Thad, and Hank, and Frank West and Frank Foster. All these guys came, you know, Eddie Jones and everybody came over there to help me out. I had a lot of expert help on that. I had never saw that before, I was pretty ignorant at that time. They walked me through that maze.
And were you happy with the results of that session?

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: the Elvin Jones group makes use of a lot of youngsters such as Nicholas Payton

ctx.x: Could you name a couple of those groups?

Young groups, you know like Terrance Blanchard, of course the Elvin Jones group makes use of a lot of youngsters such as Nicholas Payton and they even use Coltrane’s son, Ravi Coltrane with Elvin Jones. And of course Vincent Herring, an alto saxophonist, Jesse Davis, another alto saxophonist, Bobby Watson, another alto saxophonist, Roy Hargrove, Chris McBride, Antonio Hart. These are the youngsters that are, that are carrying on authentic jazz. This is not the Basie style, now, I’m talking about small group jazz.…
No, not necessarily doing the Basie thing, but in other words, just putting your thumb on the pulse and saying, are the traditions alive and well?
